---
applyTo: "maze.web/**"
---

# Web game development instructions

## Scope and native parity

The native C++ game is in `maze`, built on `ff_game_library`. `maze.web` is its TypeScript recreation using PixiJS with WebGL rendering and Web Audio, not a WebAssembly build. Preserve native gameplay, graphics, animations, sounds and controls rather than substituting approximations or changing the design. Use the native code and resources as the source of truth when changing behavior, and add source-derived regression tests. Automated checks provide substantial parity evidence, not proof of exhaustive tick-for-tick whole-game equivalence or identical native/browser PRNG sequences.

The application boots directly into the native title screen. `MR.PAC` and `MS.LILA` select both character graphics and matching maze set; never reintroduce independent maze/character selectors. Existing browser settings use the saved maze set as the selected game. Three difficulties, alternating two-player games, fruit, ghost modes, extra lives, high scores, and the original artwork/sounds are supported. Title and high-score screens use the original maze resources, bitmap font, animated Pac cursor, layout, colors, and fades through WebGL. The title background reuses the gameplay simulation with native empty difficulty, Ms. scatter behavior, no remaining pellets, no state transitions, and no audio. Native title navigation/effect sounds play after browser audio activation. The pause screen uses the original dimming, doubled red text and offset black/white shadows. Transparent HTML hit regions provide mouse/touch targeting without replacing those graphics. About is a full game-area HTML screen, not a modal: it credits Peter Spada and the primary web technologies, with selectable links and a persistent Back action. Directions/Tab select, A/Start/Enter activate, and B/Escape return to the unchanged title selection. Credits scroll independently of Back; links navigate in the same tab so controller activation does not require popup permission. Freeze the covered title simulation, allow touch scrolling only while About is visible, and preserve browser fullscreen/audio shortcuts. Browser capability/error notices remain HTML adaptations. Browser fullscreen, audio, and vibration follow device permissions/capabilities; audio starts after interaction.

The title background must leave Pac inactive, matching native `TitleScreen::GetMazePlayer()` returning an invalid player. Only the foreground menu-selection Pac cursor is visible. Ms. mode supplies ghost scatter behavior; it must not introduce a roaming Ms. Pac in the background.

Home, Resume and Pause buttons use a three-pixel white border and white icon while focused, for both keyboard and pointer focus. Keep their outer dimensions stable when focus changes.

Do not create empty files or recreate `bubble-animation.ts`. Bubble animations belong to the shared native animation player.

## Development, builds and tests

Open `maze.slnx` in Visual Studio 2026 or later. Install Node.js 22.12+ (24 LTS recommended, available on PATH) and Visual Studio's JavaScript/TypeScript project support. Restart Visual Studio if Node was just installed, reload the solution, set **maze.web** as the startup project, and press **F5**. The development server runs at http://127.0.0.1:5173. The first build restores npm dependencies and the JavaScript project SDK.

Visual Studio starts `npm run dev` during the JavaScript project's **Deploy** phase before opening Edge. Keep both **Build** and **Deploy** checked for `maze.web` in **Build > Configuration Manager** (enabled in the solution's Debug, Profile, and Release configurations). If Edge reports `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`, check **Deploy**, stop debugging, and retry F5; also check the development-server console for startup errors. Reload the solution after pulling changes to its configuration.

Terminal startup:

```powershell
Set-Location maze.web
npm ci
npm run dev
```

- `npm run build` type-checks and produces a static site in `maze.web\dist`. Deploy the contents of that directory, including `assets`. No application server or external service is required. Use `npm run preview` to serve the production build locally at http://127.0.0.1:4173; opening `index.html` directly with a `file:` URL is not supported.
- `npm test` runs deterministic gameplay, resource, audio, and storage tests. After building, `npm run test:browser` runs desktop and touch-screen tests in installed Microsoft Edge through Playwright. The headless tests use software WebGL so they can run without a physical GPU; the game itself requests WebGL normally.
- Do not run Visual Studio and npm production builds simultaneously: both write `dist`.
- Visual Studio uses the incremental `BuildWebAssets` target instead of the JavaScript SDK's unconditional build script. It tracks source/test/configuration/native-asset inputs, additions/deletions, and recorded `dist` outputs under `obj`. Unchanged builds/F5 skip production bundling; changed inputs or missing outputs rebuild normally. Keep Deploy enabled: F5 still starts Vite independently. `npm run build` remains an unconditional production build.

## Assets and saves

`predev` and `prebuild` copy PNG, WAV, JSON, and icon files directly from `maze\assets` into the ignored `maze.web\public\assets` directory. Do not edit the generated copies. The native resource definitions remain the source of truth for maze/difficulty data and sprite/animation metadata. PNG/WAV assets have not been recompressed or trimmed, avoiding a new lossy conversion during the fidelity work.

Versioned settings and high-score tables are stored locally per browser/site, not in the native Windows save format. Clearing site data removes them. No online leaderboard or account is required.

## Components and simulation

Startup uses a centered Loading... overlay and CSS spinner, styled inline in `index.html` so it appears before the JavaScript bundle downloads. Hide it after the first successful render or on startup/render failure; never leave a spinner covering an error. Respect reduced-motion preferences.

Keep safe-area-aware margins around the game in windowed and fullscreen modes. Status/error notices occupy a separate reserved row below the game, never an overlay on the maze or scores. All runtime banner messages expire after eight seconds; each new message resets that countdown, explicit clearing cancels it, and errors remain logged in the console. Fullscreen entry requires transient browser user activation; controller-only attempts must explain that the player can press F or click/tap the Full Screen option, rather than exposing a raw permission error. Clear that guidance after successful entry without clearing unrelated errors.

`main.ts` connects native screen state, input, gameplay, renderer, audio, and local storage. `screens.ts` owns the title options, high-score alphabet/navigation and native presentation coordinates. `game.ts` owns simulation state and emits events; `renderer.ts` consumes a `GameView` or `NativeScreenView` and draws PixiJS/WebGL sprites, while `audio.ts` handles sound events using Web Audio. Foreground/background screen mazes retain separate static caches. The browser's `requestAnimationFrame` drives presentation; an accumulator advances gameplay/screens at 60 fixed updates per second, independently of display refresh rate, clamping frame elapsed time to 100 ms. Rendering uses the latest state without position interpolation.

## Graphics and animations

`native-animation.ts` loads all 32 original character/effect/ghost animations from `Assets.Anim.res.json` and `Assets.GhostAnim.res.json`, expanding scoped `res:values`, templates, and references on module initialization. Vite bundles the JSON; no generated replacement animation format is maintained. The player implements the interpolation, sprite tracks, layered visuals, rotation, color/opacity, and looping/bounds used by these resources. Track interpolation follows the native engine: a visual's `method: spline` does not change its key tracks' default linear interpolation. Pac frame timing uses the selected native character animation's FPS. The 286 sprite frames retain their original PNG rectangles, repeat offsets, handles, and signed scales from `Assets.Sprites.res.json`.

Dot motion remains a subtle +/-1 logical pixel with integer tile phases. Ghost loops use their original lengths, including the third ghost's independently rotating arms; pupils look toward the pending direction with a one-pixel offset. Mouth animation freezes at walls rather than restarting, and death rotation uses continuous eighth-frame progress after the original delay. Actor/effect visibility follows the ready, caught, ghost-eaten, dying, dead, and winning transitions. The HUD includes both players' scores and the high score, original life/fruit icons, and source-colored point digits. Its native status bar is two tiles tall; life and fruit icons are anchored at tile row `totalTiles.y - 1`. Point popups remain for 55 updates after eating a ghost and 121 after eating fruit, including the update when their countdown reaches zero.

Rendering retains `AnimationSampler` instances: their output arrays, visual objects, positions, scales, and colors are borrowed and overwritten on the next sample. Do not retain/mutate these results outside their owner; use `sampleAnimation()` for independent samples. Dots share samples by the full integer tile offset, not modulo the loop length, because modulo grouping changes eight-bit tint rounding. Sprite descriptors and scalar paint transforms avoid per-sprite parsing and temporary vectors. Gameplay and title-background presentation overwrite caller-owned `Game.readView(target)` buffers; `game.view` retains independent-snapshot behavior (maze tiles remain shared as before). Use cheap scalar queries for input/state/completion, not full views. About/hidden tabs skip canvas preparation, and unchanged paused gameplay redraws only after resize/DPR/pause/context invalidation; controller polling continues. Keep `e2e\performance.spec.ts` draw-count/recovery checks and identity-based allocation regressions passing. Remaining optimization work/status is tracked in `BUGS.md`.

Title/score `view()` results, text arrays, text slots and cursor objects are borrowed reusable presentation buffers, not historical snapshots. Copy them explicitly when retaining past frames. Cache formatted scores by their values, not caller array identity. Glyph caches belong to individual pooled sprites, so variable-length/overlapping text runs cannot return stale transforms; always refresh tint, alpha and visibility. Maze geometry invalidates on board/tile storage/dimensions/offset changes, while palette and winning flashes update retained wall/floor properties. Dot lists retain original tile references and stable slots until that board cache changes; consumed pellets change kind in place, while new levels/players supply their own tile storage. Foreground pellet transforms and fade rectangles are retained. Main rendering is dirty-driven at display rate but simulation remains fixed 60 Hz: invalidate presentation for simulation updates, input/UI changes, returning from About, resize/DPR/fullscreen and context restoration. Observe the canvas as well as its host for hit-region layout; do not remeasure unchanged frames. Keep diagnostics and accessibility labels current without rewriting unchanged DOM attributes. Input reuses polling collections but action-vector ownership and native priority/hysteresis stay unchanged.

Eating dots, power pellets, fruit, and ghosts emits independent, non-looping bubbles through that same animation player, using `bubble.png` and its original handle. Instances retain their spawn positions with randomized size, playback speed, and upward drift; the native parent scale is approximately 1, not the maze sprite scale of 0.125. Each bubble grows, rises, fades, and expires instead of being drawn as a solid circle or attached to Pac. Expiry follows the native strict `frame > frame_length` check, retaining the actor at the endpoint even though these non-looping animations draw no visuals there.

## Audio

Audio references, volume, speed, and loop flags come from `Assets.Audio.res.json`. On a trusted gesture, Web Audio requests an interactive/low-latency context and decodes each unique WAV once. With sound enabled, Play waits for decoding before starting; gameplay also waits during sound enable/resume, with no catch-up updates. Ghost/fruit effects call `AudioBufferSourceNode.start()` synchronously in the same simulation update that emits the event, before drawing the result. Timed effects are never queued for late playback; premature audible playback is an explicit error. The first player's intro and original ready delay are restored. Same-named one-shots restart; background loops change only when gameplay requests a different loop. Sound off mutes the master gain; pause suspends the context. Gamepad-only startup may require a click/key to unlock browser audio, and the page displays that requirement. Browser, OS and output-device buffering (particularly Bluetooth) can still add latency; a latency hint cannot remove hardware latency.

## Controls

The Vibration option enables Gamepad API dual-rumble on the first connected controller exposing a usable vibration actuator, including Xbox controllers over Bluetooth when the browser/OS exposes haptics. Pulses retain native low/high motor strengths and durations: alternate dots (0/0.5, 100 ms), power pellets and fruit (0/1, 500 ms), moving-fruit bounces (0.5/0, 100 ms), ghosts (0.75/0, 750 ms), and death (0.375/0, 1,250 ms). Title navigation uses the same alternating dot feedback; executing settings uses the fruit-bounce feedback, including when enabling vibration. Title rumble works independently of sound, with no rumble after disabling vibration. Overlapping pulses keep the strongest unexpired value per motor. Muting audio does not disable rumble. Pause, focus loss, navigation, score entry, disconnection and disabling vibration cancel it; haptics failures are reported without stopping gameplay. Devices without usable controller haptics retain `navigator.vibrate` where available. Browser, controller firmware and Bluetooth support can limit physical fidelity; automated tests verify API calls, not physical motor output.

Arrow keys/WASD, standard gamepad stick/D-pad, or press-and-drag mouse/touch joystick on the maze control Pac. P and the native top-right pause icon pause; Escape/controller B resumes a paused game or returns an unpaused game to the title. M toggles sound and F toggles fullscreen. Title options respond to clicks/taps or Up/Down and Enter/A/Start; Left/Right cycle settings. Score entry uses the native selectable alphabet, Back and End, supports direct letter/space/period typing, and cancels without saving on Escape/B. The native Home/Play icons appear when paused. Losing focus or hiding the tab pauses the game without accumulating simulation time.

Keyboard and standard gamepads are sampled as simultaneous held axes across devices, with native Up-over-Down and Left-over-Right priority. Xbox controllers are also accepted when a browser leaves their Bluetooth profile unmapped, using the standard Xbox control indices. Sticks use the native per-direction press threshold of 0.5625 and release below 0.5; neither sticks nor D-pads discard diagonals.

Mouse/touch presses create a fixed joystick origin at the initial contact, not a target relative to Pac or a moving swipe origin. Dragging selects the original eight angular sectors beyond a radial 20-device-pixel dead zone. Keyboard/gamepad directions take priority. Input events update held state and joystick presentation immediately, but gameplay directions are applied only before fixed simulation updates, matching native input sampling. On release, only a pending turn remains; it clears when Pac takes that direction. Cancellation, lost capture, pause and focus loss discard the gesture. The original `move-arrow.png` is drawn through WebGL while dragging, using its native handle, continuous angle and distance-based scale/opacity. Its origin shares Pac's screen position: the native arrow's three-tile addition compensates for the maze's score-area translation, not a position below Pac. It disappears on release.

## Movement and gameplay regression coverage

Movement checks cover all eight corner orientations: Pac gravitates one pixel toward the new lane while moving one pixel along it, cutting diagonally ahead of ghosts, which turn only at tile centers. Tunnel checks preserve the native off-maze bounds and destinations, including the extra tile beyond the right/bottom edge when wrapping left/up. Continuing forward produces no queued ghost/fruit press, matching the native decision routine. Browser regressions inspect the rendered orange arrow pixels during real mouse and touch drags, return to origin, release and pause.

Gameplay regressions cover the native 200/400/800/1600 frightened-ghost chain across 54-update eating pauses, state-based powered artwork (separate from the speed timer), and fruit's directed-choice memories, slow-tunnel avoidance while roaming, exit targeting, random fallback, and full movement/brain reset. Route checks exercise all 160 entrance/exit combinations across the sixteen original maze variants with deterministic random draws. Ms. Pac scatter targeting is also used by the orange ghost's nearby chase fallback. House release retains the original dot quotas, post-death global quotas, inactivity timeout, and one-release-per-update rule; no artificial doorway spacing is added, so ghosts can overlap while leaving. These are source-derived regression checks, not proof of exhaustive native/web equivalence.

Expanded gameplay checks cover every difficulty row and high-level saturation for both maze sets and all three difficulties: Pac/fruit speeds, both Elroy thresholds, eyes/house/tunnel/frightened speed priority, frightened duration, flashing boundaries, and complete scatter/chase schedules. Fixed-point checks include negative pellet delays, residual fractions, multi-pixel collision checks, and the different accumulator behavior while eating ghosts. An additional audit compiled the original C++ movement/brain methods and compared 24,378,496 Pac, ghost, house-return and fruit movement cases across all sixteen maze variants with matching controlled random choices; those cases had no remaining mismatches. This does not establish identical native/browser PRNG sequences or exhaustive whole-game equivalence.

## Progression and bonuses

Native progression timing is preserved with separate initial, player-announcement and READY phases: P1 starts on update 273, P2 and restarted lives on update 122. New P1 levels repeat the announcement without replaying the opening intro. Nonfatal player switches advance the destination player on the switching update. A fatal life freezes for 120 updates with the native red player/game-over messages before score entry; switching or final game completion occurs on the following update. After the final switch, the global GAME OVER screen remains for the native 120 simulation updates (`gameOverCounter > 120`) before returning to the menu; this is fixed-step based, not wall-clock based. Lives, the first/repeat extra-life thresholds, and the lifetime extra-life cap are resolved from the selected maze-set and difficulty definition in `Values.Mazes.res.json`. Bonuses are checked once after maze advancement, before life/level handling: first at 10,000, then every 10,000 on easy/normal or 20,000 on hard, with three awarded extra lives on easy and two on normal/hard. The native four-life cap is retained; crossing a threshold at the cap advances that threshold and plays its sound without consuming the award quota.

## High scores

High-score categories use selected game/maze set and difficulty, independently of player count. The native title shows ten seven-column scores and nine-character names for the keyboard/controller-selected Mr./Ms. game; other selected options hide the table, just like native. Names retain the native nine-character alphabet (letters, spaces and periods), including blank entries displayed as `---`; score entry can be skipped without saving. Entry uses `high-score-maze`, the seven-column alphabet grid, magenta selected letter/preview, blinking dashes, Back and End. The frozen game dims to 0.875 in 1/64 steps before the score foreground appears, then fades back before resuming. Equal scores follow earlier ties, and tying the tenth-place score does not qualify. Queued multiplayer entries requalify against the updated table. Existing browser saves migrate names without dropping their scores. A pause request from focus/visibility loss or WebGL interruption during entry or either fade must survive closing the screen: require explicit resume before the next player advances, even if focus/graphics recovered before the fade finished.

`test\game-over.test.ts` runs complete collision-driven matches for both characters, every difficulty, solo play and both multiplayer elimination orders. `e2e\game-over.spec.ts` bundles the real application in memory with test-only fixtures and a manual frame scheduler; it does not replace the game, renderer, input or storage. It exercises actual collisions/death transitions, independent player scores/levels, full-table boundaries and ties, save/cancel and duplicate input, keyboard/controller/touch editing, reload/write failures, and focus/tab/WebGL interruptions. Fixtures seed scores, lives and levels and remove pellets to isolate lifecycle behavior; they do not verify earning those scores through ordinary play. The hooks and fast clock never enter the production bundle. Run these browser cases with `npm run test:browser -- 'game-over\.spec'` after building.
